newsitem.title: UK: British economy shows signs of struggle.
newsitem.headline: British economy shows signs of struggle.

text.p: Britain's manufacturers suffered a surprising fall in output in November, official figures issued Friday showed, while evidence is mounting that Christmas retail sales fell short of expectations.
Manufacturing output fell 0.5 percent in November, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, confounding economists' forecasts that production would jump by about 0.3 percent.

That slide in activity, coupled with evidence of lacklustre Christmas sales, could take the pressure off Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates soon to keep the economy under control, analysts said.
The government dismissed the month-on-month fall in output as a blip, preferring to look at the underlying trend.
"There is a continuing steady increase in production, in spite of monthly figures that can be erratic," said Angela Knight, Economic Secretary to the Treasury.

Industrial production, which measures output of the manufacturing sector plus energy production, rose 0.5 percent on the month. But that was largely due to a 5 percent rise in electricity, gas and water output due to a cold weather snap.
The ONS said the majority of manufacturing sectors were hit. Friday's figures showed output was only 0.2 percent higher than in November the previous year.
But economists tended to back the government's line that the drop would prove to be an abberation.
"One is often reluctant to agree with the Treasury but I think the trend probably still is up, albeit modestly," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
James Barty, chief UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, pointed to a 0.4 percent increase in output in the three months to November from the prior period.
"What the underlying figures are telling you is that the trend is still up for manufacturing output and I expect that to continue, at least in the short term," he said.
The ONS said there was little evidence that the drop in production was solely due to the strong British pound -- up 14 percent in six months -- hitting exports.
But given that exporters will start to feel the pinch from the pound sooner or later, they are far from out of the woods.

Certainly, Chancellor Clarke will sieze on Friday's data to argue that base rates, at 6 percent, are high enough for now. He holds his monthly monetary policy meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George next Wednesday.
His case has been strengthened by a rash of evidence that Christmas retail sales fell short of boom-time expectations.
The Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey, released overnight, showed many retailers suffered subdued Christmas sales.

The CBI's survey found 52 percent of retail firms reported higher sales year-on-year in December, while 19 percent said sales fell -- a positive balance of 33 percent but well below November's reading of 48 percent.

Trading statements from Britain's large retail groups also painted a mixed picture. On Friday, consumer goods and homewear retailer Argos Plc issued a profit warning and said sales in the second half of the year were lower than expected.
Stores group Sears Plc Thursday said Christmas sales had been disappointing, adding that annual profits would be below last year's levels.
Few economists expect retail spending to dry up. Most forecast growth of more than 4 percent this year. But this week's figures could well defer an interest rate rise.
"These figures swing the odds against a rise in rates in a week's time," Shepperd said. But he still forecast a tightening in February.
